questions.question:
**In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and click the option corresponding to it. If the sentence is free from error, click the "No error" option.**

Three summons have been (1)/ issued by the district court (2)/ but he has not turned up yet. (3)/ No Error (4)
questions.solution: ‘Summons’ is a singular noun and its plural form is ‘summonses’. Therefore, the error lies in the first part of the sentence as the number ‘three’ indicates that more than one summons was issued.

questions.question:
**In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and click the option corresponding to it. If the sentence is free from error, click the "No error" option.**

Aayushi has come (1)/ here to do a master (2)/ degree in Social Work. (3)/ No Error (4)
questions.solution:
The correct answer is** '2'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The error lies in part 2 of the sentence. The phrase "do a master" is incorrect in this context. The appropriate wording should be "do a master's".
 
• The term "master's" is a shortened form of "master's degree". This form indicates possession or belonging, essentially conveying that it is the degree of a master level of study.
 
• The correct sentence should read, "Aayushi has come here to do a master's degree in Social Work."
 
• This adjustment makes the phrase grammatically correct and aligns with the standard way of referring to graduate-level academic degrees in English.

Therefore, the correct answer is **'Option 2'.**

**The sentence(s) given with blanks are to be filled with an appropriate word(s). Four alternatives are suggested for each question. For each question, choose the correct alternative and click the button corresponding to it.**

questions.solution:

questions.solution:
Here the correct answer is **Misappropriated**.

questions.solution: The sentence means that ‘he’ was there in front of or in the presence of Ankita, but could not speak anything for some time. **In the following question, out of the four alternatives, choose the word which best expresses the meaning of the given word and click the button corresponding to it.**

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **wander**.

__
 
• The word **"meander"** means to follow a winding or intricate course; to wander aimlessly. (घूमना)

 
 
• **Example: **The river **meanders **through the valley, creating beautiful scenery.
 
 
 
• **"Wander" **refers to moving without a fixed course, aim, or goal; to roam. (भटकना)
 
 
• **Example: **He loves to **wander **through the old city streets, discovering hidden gems.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Option 3**.

• **Futile** (व्यर्थ): Incapable of producing any useful result; pointless.
 
 
• **Example:** His attempts to change her mind were **futile**.

questions.question:
**Below are three alternatives which may be used to improve the sentence by replacing the words given in the brackets. You may choose option 1, 2 or 3. In case no improvement is needed, choose 4.**

Hardly had I finished cooking dinner (before) Rajesh arrived.

questions.question:
**Below are three alternatives which may be used to improve the sentence by replacing the words given in the brackets. You may choose option 1, 2 or 3. In case no improvement is needed, choose 4.**

I met the two boys, (whom I believe are) twins.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option (2).**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The word **"who"** is correctly used as a relative pronoun in this sentence. It introduces a relative clause **("who I believe are twins")** that provides more information about the antecedent, which in this case is "the two boys."
 
• Relative pronouns such as** "who"** relate to the noun they modify and act within their clause as a subject or object. In this sentence, "who" serves as the subject of the verb "are," correctly linking the verb to the two boys implied by **"who."**
 
• **Let's break the sentence: **
 
 
• I met the two boys, who are twins, I believe it.
 
 
 
• The choice of **"who" **over "whom" is grounded in the function of "who" within the clause. Since it acts as the subject of the verb "are," "who" is the appropriate choice. "Whom" would be used if the relative pronoun were the object of the clause or of a preposition.

Therefore, the correct answer is **"who I believe are"**

**Corrected sentence is: ***I met the two boys, who I believe are twins.*

questions.question:
**Below are three alternatives which may be used to improve the sentence by replacing the words given in the brackets. You may choose option 1, 2 or 3. In case no improvement is needed, choose 4.**

Let's buy a new phone with the annual bonus, (can we)?
questions.solution:
‘Can we’ should be replaced with ‘shall we’ because imperative sentences for suggestions starting with 'Let' take question tags starting with 'shall'.

Note that in other type of sentences, if the statement is positive, the tag must be negative and vice- versa.

E.G. *You live in Delhi, don’t you?*

 *You haven’t completed the assignment, have you?*

questions.question: Man and his _____ are two distinct things,
questions.solution: From the latter part of the sentence, it is clear that ‘deed’ is the correct fit for the blank space.

questions.question: whereas a good deed should call forth approbation and a _____ deed, disapprobation,
questions.solution: Note that the word ‘disapprobation’ is mentioned after the blank space. If good should call forth approbation, it must be bad or wicked deed which should call for disapprobation. Thus, option 1 is the best fit answer.

questions.question: the doer of the deed whether good or _______
questions.solution: The usage of the word ‘whether’ indicates that two words which are opposite in meaning should be mentioned. If one of the words is ‘good’, the other one should be ‘bad’. Since ‘bad’ is present among the options, do not mark ‘evil’ as the answer.

questions.question: always deserves _____ or pity as the case may be.
questions.solution: The usage of the phrase ‘as the case may be’ indicates that what people deserve depends on the kind of deed they do. So if a person who commits bad deed deserves ‘pity’, a person who performs good deeds should be ‘respected’. Option 1 carries an opposite meaning and the other two options are not as apt as ‘respect’.

questions.question: is rarely _____ and that is why the poison of hatred spreads in the world.
questions.solution: The concerned sentence mentions the idea of ‘Hate the sin and not the sinner’, which it says is easy to understand. We need an action in relation to the precept, the lack of which spreads the poison of hatred in the world. So even if you understand an idea but do not **practise** or perform it, it can have the above mentioned consequence. Thus, option 2 is the best fit answer. ‘Following’ and ‘acknowledging’ are not same as ‘practising’.

questions.solution: With reference to superstitions, the passage mentions: *They are unreasoned and **irrational** beliefs that gradually become matters of faith*. So statement 3 is incorrect with respect to the passage. The other statements are correct.

questions.question: According to passage which of the following is not regarded as a superstition by the people?

options.text: crossing of path by black cat

questions.question: What can only be the effective counter of superstition?

options.text: belief in the sanctity of time
awareness through plays like Julius Caesar by Shakespeare
a broad light of scientific discovery

questions.solution: The passage mentions that *growth of superstitions were the direct outcome of the lack of scientific advancement.* So ‘a broad light of scientific discovery’ can be the effective counter of superstition as scientific discoveries are based on rationality. The other options are either incorrect or are out of the context of the given passage.
